clinicalPearls: H. pylori has a proven etiologic role in peptic ulcer disease; together with NSAID use it is one of the two most common causes of gastroduodenal ulcers (p.302).

In dyspeptic patients under 60 with no alarm features, test-and-treat is the recommended initial strategy: assess H. pylori status by fecal (stool) antigen or urea breath testing, and treat those who are positive (p.303).
Eradication of H. pylori in patients with bleeding ulcers lowers rebleeding rates to under 5% (p.272).
H. pylori is a known driver of gastric cancer; the intestinal subtype of gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with H. pylori infection and atrophic/atopic gastritis (p.646, p.647).
Although H. pylori is extremely common (present in roughly half of all humans), gastric cancer develops in only a small subset of those infected, so infection alone is not sufficient (p.646).

Treating H. pylori reduces future gastric cancer risk: eradication lowered gastric cancer incidence in people with a first-degree relative who had gastric cancer, and reduced second cancers in patients with prior early-stage gastric cancer (p.646).
All patients with gastric lymphoma should have H. pylori status evaluated; if histopathology is negative, confirm with a stool antigen test or urea breath test (p.649).

For gastric MALT lymphoma, antibiotic eradication of H. pylori alone is highly effective and is the initial therapy when H. pylori is positive and the t(11;18) translocation assay is negative, producing high response and complete-remission rates (p.649-650).
harrison.pathophysiology: H. pylori is a flagellated gastric bacterium whose colonization triggers chronic mucosal inflammation. The flagellum lets the organism access the gastric epithelium and is essential for virulence; H. pylori evades innate immunity by producing a flagellin epitope that does not bind TLR5 and tetra-acylated LPS that does not activate TLR4 (p.1009-1010). Adhesion and gastric tropism are mediated by bacterial outer-membrane proteins BabA and SabA interacting with epithelial GM1 ganglioside (p.1009). Chronic H. pylori inflammation, partly via generation of carcinogenic nitrites from dietary nitrates, drives the gastritis-to-cancer sequence and is a recognized cause of peptic ulcer disease, gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal subtype), and gastric MALT lymphoma; certain higher-virulence strains carry greater cancer risk (p.646).
additionalInvestigations: Urea breath test (noninvasive) for active infection and for confirming eradication.
Stool (fecal) antigen test (noninvasive) for active infection and eradication confirmation.
Endoscopic biopsy with histopathology, including for gastric lymphoma staging.
PCR or FISH for the t(11;18) translocation in gastric MALT lymphoma to predict responsiveness to eradication therapy (p.649).
redFlags: Dyspepsia with alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding/anemia, jaundice, palpable mass or adenopathy, family history of gastroesophageal malignancy) or age over 60 warrants upper endoscopy to exclude malignancy rather than test-and-treat alone (p.302-303).
Failure to respond to eradication, or recurrent/refractory symptoms, should prompt further evaluation.
harrison.prognosis: Eradication markedly improves ulcer outcomes (rebleeding falls below 5%). In gastric MALT lymphoma, H. pylori eradication yields high response rates with complete remission in the majority, though time to remission can be prolonged (averaging ~15-16 months in some studies), requiring patient monitoring before declaring non-response (p.272, p.650). Benefit in functional dyspepsia is limited but statistically significant (about a 9% risk reduction vs placebo) (p.302).
pitfalls: PITFALL: PPIs and other acid-suppressing drugs can cause false-negative urea breath and stool antigen tests; acid suppression must be stopped before testing for active H. pylori infection.
Confirmation of eradication should be performed 4-6 weeks after completing therapy, not immediately (p.303).
Do not rely on a single negative histopathology result in gastric lymphoma; confirm with noninvasive stool antigen or urea breath testing (p.649).

NEGATION: Even H. pylori-negative MALT tumors may respond to anti-H. pylori therapy, so a negative test does not preclude a trial of eradication; the t(11;18) translocation identifies a subgroup less likely to respond (p.649-650).
NEGATION: H. pylori eradication does NOT worsen GERD symptoms, despite H. pylori infection being associated with a reduced prevalence of GERD (p.302).
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e, Chapter 168 (Helicobacter pylori Infections), p.1298.

management: First-line eradication with a proton pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics (clarithromycin-based triple therapy with amoxicillin or metronidazole), reserving bismuth-based quadruple therapy for areas of high clarithromycin resistance or after failure
Guide antibiotic selection by local resistance patterns and susceptibility testing, using salvage regimens such as levofloxacin-containing therapy for persistent infection
Continue acid suppression with a proton pump inhibitor to promote healing of any associated peptic ulcer
Use eradication as first-line treatment for gastric MALT lymphoma, referring to haematology-oncology for radiotherapy or systemic therapy if t(11;18)-positive or non-responsive
Confirm cure after therapy with a urea breath test or stool antigen test, having stopped the proton pump inhibitor, rather than relying on serology
Manage bleeding ulcers endoscopically and eradicate the organism to reduce rebleeding, and offer endoscopic surveillance of premalignant atrophic gastritis
